items_missed: No agenda statement: opened with "I am going to break down the pricing structure for you" but never gave the ~10-15 minute timeframe and never asked for confirmation, so there was no "Sound good?" checkpoint before a 6-minute pricing monologue.
Never used the "pricing is super simple" opener - went straight into hourly rate, overnight fee and trip fee, which is the densest possible entry point on a two-day move.

"No hidden fees" was asserted but never itemized - "Aside from those fees there's no other additional or hidden fees" with no mention of no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees.
What's-included list was incomplete: covered taxes, insurance, pad wrap, floor and door protection, but skipped gas, truck, bands and tools.
Gave firm point estimates (9 hours day one, 4.5 hours day two, "approximately $8,100") instead of a typical time range for the home size - no range language anywhere on a long-haul two-day move.
Estimate variables left out entirely: stairs or elevator at either address, specialty items, walk distance, and traffic on a Dallas-to-Leander drive where drive time is a billable hour block.
No equivalents or reference points used (school bus, etc.) to help the customer sanity-check a two-truck, four-mover job.
Save Your Ass had the payoff line but none of the substance - zero consolidation examples (kids' toys, garden tools, loose items in drawers, photos off walls) and no "take a carload" tip.
Insurance explanation stopped at the $2,000 No Worries coverage - no 60 cents per pound baseline, so the customer has no sense of what the coverage is an upgrade from.

Never asked Michael to reply to the confirmation email with corrections, and never mentioned the bolded detail list at the top of the email - a real gap, because Michael explicitly asked "are you gonna send another copy of this or estimate" and was unsure which emailed quote to keep.

The customer's live risk - sellers may not vacate before the 15th - was acknowledged ("Yeah, understood") but never converted into a plan: no hold date, no cutoff for when Michael needs to call, no confirmation of what a one-day slip actually costs him.
Never asked any version of "is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?" even though the customer volunteered a bad prior-move story about a seller who hadn't moved out.
Said "the seventeenth is not available" when the move under discussion was the 15th and 16th, which left the alternate-branch offer confusing rather than reassuring.
Gave the branch phone number but no business hours.
top_strength: The clock explanation was the best part of this call, and it is genuinely hard to deliver on a two-day move. Nick walked the clock starting when the movers arrive on day one, stopping when the crew reaches the Leander hotel, restarting when they leave the hotel on day two, and ending when everything is unloaded "and you all are happy where everything is" - then layered the 2.5-hour daily minimum and 15-minute prorated increments on top and closed with "Does that make sense?" He also landed the On-Time Guarantee with real teeth: "if we arrive even a minute outside that window will automatically discount your move," tied to the industry's late-and-cancel reputation. The booking close was clean - no deposits or rescheduling fees, then a direct "you want me to go ahead and get you on the schedule for the fifteenth and sixteenth."
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: stop quoting a single number. Nick anchored Michael on "approximately $8,100" with no range, which is exactly how a booking estimate ends up outside the 20% band. He should have said: "For a home this size on a two-day move we typically see day one land between eight and ten hours, so plan on a budget of roughly $7,700 to $8,600 - and the things that push it to the top of that range are stairs, long walks to the truck, and traffic on the drive down." Same information, but it sets an honest band and pre-explains the variables instead of leaving them to surface on move day. Second priority: the Save Your Ass speech is half-built. Nick had the payoff - "everything is just packed organized as best you can, that'll help out the efficiency and save you money at the end of the day" - but gave no examples, and examples are the whole point. Add: "Box up the loose stuff in drawers, get the kids' toys and garden tools into bins, take the photos off the walls, and anything small and awkward, throw a carload in your own car - every trip the guys don't make is billable time you don't pay for." Third: Michael asked twice which email to keep and never got a clear answer - close every booking with "the confirmation email has your key details bolded at the top, give it a read and reply with any corrections," because on this move the seller-vacancy risk makes a written date on the record worth more than usual.
phone_presence_notes: Used "Michael" throughout, reacted genuinely to the customer's bad-realtor story ("Oh, wow." "Jees."), apologized for cutting him off, and self-aware enough to say "I've done a lot of talking I appreciate you listen to all that" - warm, but the call is heavily rep-monologue with the customer reduced to "Mm-hmm."
audio_review_reason: Scored 4 on warm language, but the customer's side is almost entirely "Mm-hmm" against several minutes of uninterrupted rep monologue, and the transcript has overlap artifacts in the pricing stretch - want audio to confirm the customer was actually tracking the numbers rather than passively acknowledging them.
